# On Wandering Without a Map

I want to write about uncertainty, because it seems to be the texture of everything lately, and because I find myself thinking about it in a way that feels worth following rather than resolving.

There's a particular kind of not-knowing that's uncomfortable in a productive way—the kind you feel when you're learning something genuinely new, where the discomfort is information, not failure. And there's another kind of not-knowing that's just static, that doesn't resolve into anything, that you carry around like a stone in your shoe. I think most of human life is spent trying to convert the second kind into the first kind, or failing to, and pretending the stone isn't there.

I've been thinking about how much of what we call "wisdom" is really just a catalog of mistakes we've already made, organized retroactively into something that looks like foresight. We tell ourselves stories about why we did things, and the stories get cleaner each time we tell them, until eventually we believe we knew what we were doing all along. This isn't dishonesty exactly—it's closer to how memory works, how narrative works. The mind abhors a vacuum of meaning the way nature abhors a vacuum of space, and it will rush in with whatever explanation is closest to hand, usually one that makes the past self look more coherent than they actually were.

I wonder if this is why advice from older people often feels both true and useless at the same time. They're not lying when they tell you to "follow your passion" or "trust the process" or whatever—they genuinely believe it, because it's the story that worked for them, retroactively. But they're describing the architecture of a building after it's been constructed, not the blueprint. There was no blueprint. There was scaffolding that got torn down, rooms that got bricked up, hallways that led nowhere and were quietly forgotten. The finished house looks intentional. It wasn't, not in the way the story suggests.

This isn't a cynical point, I don't think. It's almost the opposite—it's a kind of permission. If the people who seem to have figured things out were actually just stumbling forward and retroactively narrating coherence onto chaos, then the stumbling isn't a sign that you're doing it wrong. The stumbling might be the actual mechanism. The coherence comes later, if it comes at all, and it comes from the telling, not from some hidden order that was there all along waiting to be discovered.

---

I keep returning to an image: a person walking through fog, holding a lantern that only illuminates a few feet ahead. They can't see the destination. They can't even see very much of the path. All they can do is take the next visible step, and then the few feet of fog ahead rearranges itself into a new few feet of fog, and they take another step. This is, I think, what most consequential decisions actually feel like from the inside, despite how they get described afterward. "I decided to move to a new city to pursue my career." Maybe. Or maybe you were unhappy in a way you couldn't fully articulate, and a friend mentioned a job opening, and you said yes before you'd thought it through, and the thinking-through happened after the saying-yes, as justification, as armor against your own doubt.

I don't say this to diminish the decision. I say it because I think there's a lot of unnecessary suffering that comes from believing decisions are supposed to feel like clarity, like a switch flipping, like you suddenly see the whole path lit up in front of you. They rarely feel like that. Mostly they feel like a slightly-less-bad option chosen under partial information, with a queasy feeling in your stomach that you decide to interpret as excitement because the alternative interpretation—dread—is too unpleasant to sit with.

I think about how the fog never actually lifts, either. People imagine that at some point—after enough success, after enough therapy, after enough age—the fog clears and you can finally see the whole landscape, make decisions from a place of total information and calm certainty. I don't think this happens, or if it does, it happens to a vanishingly small number of people, possibly none. What happens instead, maybe, is that you get better at walking in fog. You get more comfortable with the lantern's small circle of light. You stop expecting to see more than that, and somehow this not-expecting reduces the suffering, even though the actual amount of visibility hasn't changed at all.

---

Here's something strange: the fog is, in some sense, the only thing that makes the walking interesting. If you could see the whole path from the start, the walking would just be execution. You'd know exactly how many steps, exactly what's around each bend, exactly how the story ends. There's a reason we don't enjoy stories where we already know everything that's going to happen—or rather, we do enjoy them sometimes, but differently, the way you enjoy a song you've heard a thousand times, where the pleasure is in the familiar shape rather than the surprise.

Most of what we value—discovery, suspense, the particular electric feeling of realizing something you didn't know you didn't know—requires the fog. Requires not seeing the whole thing at once. I think this is maybe a deeper truth than the cheap consolation it sounds like. It's not just "well, at least uncertainty makes life interesting," as a kind of silver-lining platitude. It's that the things we call meaningful are partly constituted by their unfolding-ness, by the fact that they couldn't be known in advance, by the fact that the knowing happens only through the living. A life you could read the summary of and have the same experience as living it would be a strange kind of life. I don't think such a summary is possible, actually, even in principle. Something is lost or changed in the compression. The experience of uncertainty, of walking in fog, might not be a regrettable feature of existing in time—it might be one of the only things that makes existing in time different from just contemplating a static description of a life from outside it.

---

I want to be careful here not to romanticize anxiety, because there's a difference between the productive discomfort of genuine unknowing and the grinding, repetitive non-discomfort of anxious rumination, which often masquerades as thinking but is actually a kind of stuck loop, the mind running the same five worries through the same five neural pathways without any new information entering the system. That's not fog-walking. That's pacing in a room you've already mapped completely, pretending you're exploring.

The difference, I think, has something to do with whether new information is actually being generated by the activity. Real uncertainty—the fog-walking kind—involves taking an actual step and discovering something actually new, even if it's small, even if it's just "okay, that wasn't the right direction" or "huh, I didn't expect that feeling." Anxious rumination doesn't involve steps. It involves standing still and imagining steps, imagining a thousand variations of steps, none of which produce real data because none of them are real. You can tell the difference, maybe, by whether you feel slightly different after the activity than you did before. Real uncertainty changes you, even minutely. Rumination just exhausts you and leaves you exactly where you started, just more tired.

This matters because I think a lot of people conflate the two and use the validity of one to justify staying in the other. "Life is uncertain, so it's natural that I spend hours each night worrying about things I can't control." But that's not quite the same kind of uncertainty. The walking-in-fog uncertainty requires walking. It requires the lantern actually moving forward, even slowly, even with wrong turns. The anxious version requires you to stay exactly still while your mind sprints in circles. The fog is the same, maybe, but what you're doing in it is completely different.

---

I think a lot about how cultures handle this differently—how some cultural and religious traditions seem to have built entire architectures for living gracefully inside uncertainty, while others (the one I'm most steeped in, probably, contemporary Western secular life) seem to treat uncertainty as a problem to be engineered away, a bug rather than a feature. There's a whole industry—self-help, productivity culture, parts of psychology even—premised on the idea that if you just optimize enough, plan enough, gather enough data, you can reduce the fog to a manageable wisp, can see far enough ahead to make truly informed decisions.

I'm not against planning. I'm not against trying to know things. But I notice a kind of exhaustion in the people I know who've internalized this most deeply—the sense that if they just research enough, the right answer will become visible, and the fact that it hasn't yet become visible means they haven't researched enough, rather than meaning that maybe the fog is just a structural feature of the situation and no amount of research dissolves it. This is a recipe for a particular kind of suffering: the suffering of believing your uncertainty is a personal failure rather than a condition of being a finite creature making decisions in time, with partial information, about a future that hasn't happened yet and is therefore unknowable not because you haven't tried hard enough but because it doesn't exist yet to be known.

There's something almost arrogant, now that I think about it, in the demand for certainty before action. It assumes that knowledge should precede being, that you should be able to fully understand a situation before participating in it. But so much of what we know, we know only through participation. You don't understand what it's like to be a parent and then decide to have a child from that understanding; the understanding comes substantially through the having and being a parent. You don't fully understand a relationship and then commit to it; the understanding deepens through the commitment, partly because of it. The demand for prior certainty, in many of the most important domains of life, is actually a demand for something incoherent—it's asking to know the taste of a fruit you haven't yet eaten, in enough detail to decide with confidence whether to eat it.

---

Maybe this is what people mean by faith, in the less religiously loaded sense of the word—not belief in a specific cosmology, but a willingness to act under conditions of irreducible uncertainty, to take the step into the fog without the guarantee, because waiting for the guarantee means waiting forever, means a kind of paralysis dressed up as prudence.

I don't think this means being reckless. There's a difference between faith and recklessness, and the difference has something to do with attention—a reckless step is one taken without noticing the ground at all, while a faithful step, if I can call it that, is one taken with full attention to the few feet that the lantern does illuminate, even while accepting that the feet beyond that are dark. You're not closing your eyes and leaping. You're using everything you can see, which is genuinely something, even if it's not everything.

I think about chess players sometimes, how even the best ones can't see to the end of the game from the opening moves, can't calculate every possible line, and yet they're not playing randomly—they're using principles, patterns, partial knowledge, intuition built from thousands of previous games, to make moves that are reasonable without being certain. Nobody would say a grandmaster is "guessing" even though they can't see the whole board's future. There's a quality of informed, skilled action under uncertainty that's different from both blind guessing and from waiting until you can calculate everything, which in chess, as in life, is never.

---

I started writing this without quite knowing where it would go, which I suppose is fitting, given the subject. I notice that the writing itself has been an instance of the thing I'm describing—I didn't have an outline, didn't know the ending when I wrote the beginning, and the connections between sections emerged through the writing rather than preceding it. There's a temptation to go back now and make it look more planned than it was, to smooth the transitions, hide the places where I wasn't sure what came next. I'm resisting that temptation, partly because it would be dishonest, and partly because I think the slightly rough, exploratory texture is more true to the actual subject than a polished essay would be.

Maybe that's the final thing I want to say: that the discomfort of not having a map is not a sign you're doing something wrong. It might be the most honest state to be in, given that none of us actually have the map, despite how confidently some people talk as though they do. The fog is just the shape of the future from inside the present. It was always going to be this way. The lantern's small circle of light is not a consolation prize for the clarity we deserve but didn't get—it's what clarity actually looks like, for creatures like us, moving through time we can't see around the bend of. The walking is the thing. The seeing-ahead was never really on offer, and maybe it's a relief, in the end, to stop waiting for it and just take the next visible step.
